claim: Several spontaneous mouse mutants with deficits in motor coordination and associated cerebellar neuropathology have been described.
source: Several spontaneous mouse mutants with deficits in motor coordination and associated cerebellar neuropathology have been described.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Both visible gait alterations and neuroanatomical abnormalities throughout the brain differ across mutants.
source: Intriguingly, both visible gait alterations and neuroanatomical abnormalities throughout the brain differ across mutants.
evidence: This statement is supported by the comparative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: LocoMouse system was previously used to quantify specific deficits in locomotor coordination in mildly ataxic Purkinje cell degeneration mice (pcd).
source: We previously used the LocoMouse system to quantify specific deficits in locomotor coordination in mildly ataxic Purkinje cell degeneration mice (pcd; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to previously published work by the authors.

claim: Direct comparison of locomotor kinematics and linear discriminant analysis reveal a surprisingly similar pattern of impairments in multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination in reeler and pcd mutants.
source: Despite clearly visible gait differences, direct comparison of locomotor kinematics and linear discriminant analysis reveal a surprisingly similar pattern of impairments in multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination in the two mutants.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Visibly ataxic mouse mutants exhibit varying patterns of neuropathology throughout the brain.
source: Visibly ataxic mouse mutants exhibit varying patterns of neuropathology throughout the brain (Cendelin, 2014; Fortier et al., 1987; Goldowitz et al., 1997; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019; Mullen et al., 1976; Walter et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Motor coordination deficits in ataxic mutants are generally attributed to abnormal cell patterning within the cerebellum.
source: Although their motor coordination deficits are generally attributed to abnormal cell patterning within the cerebellum (Arshavsky et al., 1983; Orlovsky et al., 1999), these lines have distinct patterning defects within the cerebellum, varying degrees of extracerebellar involvement, and differences in age of onset (Cendelin, 2014; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by citations.

claim: Ataxic mutant lines have distinct patterning defects within the cerebellum, varying degrees of extracerebellar involvement, and differences in age of onset.
source: Although their motor coordination deficits are generally attributed to abnormal cell patterning within the cerebellum (Arshavsky et al., 1983; Orlovsky et al., 1999), these lines have distinct patterning defects within the cerebellum, varying degrees of extracerebellar involvement, and differences in age of onset (Cendelin, 2014; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The nature of the motor deficits exhibited by ataxic mice varies and can often be distinguished by trained observers.
source: The nature of the motor deficits exhibited by these mice also varies, and can often be distinguished by trained observers (Berman, 2018; Brooks and Dunnett, 2009; Hoogland et al., 2015; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019; Schiffmann et al., 1999; Stroobants et al., 2013; Vinueza Veloz et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Analysis of motor coordination is often limited to low dimensional descriptions of limited specificity that fail to distinguish between related behavioral phenotypes.
source: However, analysis of motor coordination is often limited to low dimensional descriptions of limited specificity that fail to distinguish between related behavioral phenotypes (Brooks and Dunnett, 2009; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019).
evidence: This is a critique of existing methods supported by citations.

claim: Analysis of locomotor kinematics can provide higher dimensional readouts of locomotor behavior.
source: Analysis of locomotor kinematics can provide higher dimensional readouts of locomotor behavior (Cendelín et al., 2010; Gabriel et al., 2009; Zörner et al., 2010), but can still suffer from a lack of specificity due to an abundance of highly correlated measures that ultimately reflect non-specific features such as changes in walking speed or body size (Batka et al., 2014; Cendelín et al., 2010; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Locomotor kinematic analysis can suffer from a lack of specificity due to an abundance of highly correlated measures that ultimately reflect non-specific features such as changes in walking speed or body size.
source: Analysis of locomotor kinematics can provide higher dimensional readouts of locomotor behavior (Cendelín et al., 2010; Gabriel et al., 2009; Zörner et al., 2010), but can still suffer from a lack of specificity due to an abundance of highly correlated measures that ultimately reflect non-specific features such as changes in walking speed or body size (Batka et al., 2014; Cendelín et al., 2010; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological critique supported by citations.

claim: Locomotor deficits in pcd mice were restricted to specific aspects of multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination, while the forward trajectories of individual paws were spared.
source: We found that locomotor deficits in pcd were restricted to specific aspects of multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination, while the forward trajectories of individual paws were spared (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The tail movements of pcd mice reflected the passive consequences of limb movement.
source: We further found that the tail movements of pcd mice reflected the passive consequences of limb movement (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Reeler mice are a classic ataxic mutant.
source: Reeler mice are a classic ataxic mutant (Cendelin, 2014; Curran and D'Arcangelo, 1998; D'Arcangelo et al., 1999; D'Arcangelo et al., 1995; Falconer, 1951) with an autosomal recessive mutation in the reelin gene, which is important for neural cell migration (Beckers et al., 1994; Hack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reeler mice have an autosomal recessive mutation in the reelin gene, which is important for neural cell migration.
source: Reeler mice are a classic ataxic mutant (Cendelin, 2014; Curran and D'Arcangelo, 1998; D'Arcangelo et al., 1999; D'Arcangelo et al., 1995; Falconer, 1951) with an autosomal recessive mutation in the reelin gene, which is important for neural cell migration (Beckers et al., 1994; Hack et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a well-established genetic fact supported by citations.

claim: Loss of reelin causes several defects, in particular aberrant localization of neurons and failure of neuronal layer formation.
source: Its loss causes several defects, in particular aberrant localization of neurons and failure of neuronal layer formation.
evidence: This is a known consequence of reelin mutation supported by the context and citations.

claim: Several brain regions are affected in reeler mice, including cerebellum, hippocampus, neocortex, inferior olive and substantia nigra.
source: Several brain regions are affected, including cerebellum (Hamburgh, 1963; Terashima et al., 1983), hippocampus (Stanfield et al., 1979), neocortex (Mikoshiba et al., 1980), inferior olive (Blatt and Eisenman, 1988) and substantia nigra (Kang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Neuropathology in reeler mice is particularly striking within the cerebellum, where severe irregularities in cellular localization are also associated with corresponding aberrant synaptic connectivity between cell types, abnormal foliation, and hypoplasia.
source: Neuropathology in these mice is particularly striking within the cerebellum, where severe irregularities in cellular localization are also associated with corresponding aberrant synaptic connectivity between cell types, abnormal foliation, and hypoplasia.
evidence: This is a description of known anatomical features of reeler mice.

claim: Homozygous reeler mutants have been described as having a severely ataxic, 'reeling' gait, with difficulties in maintaining their hindquarters upright.
source: Although their locomotor kinematics and whole-body coordination have not been reported, homozygous reeler mutants have been described as having a severely ataxic, 'reeling' gait, with difficulties in maintaining their hindquarters upright (Cendelin, 2014; Lalonde et al., 2004; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019).
evidence: This is a description from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Reeler mice exhibit poor performance in rotarod, stationary beam and water maze tests.
source: Like most ataxic mutants, reelers also exhibit poor performance in rotarod, stationary beam and water maze tests (Lalonde et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: pcd and reeler mice share grossly abnormal cerebellar circuitry, but exhibit marked differences in synaptic connectivity within the cerebellum and across the brain.
source: Thus, pcd and reeler mice share grossly abnormal cerebellar circuitry, but exhibit marked differences in synaptic connectivity within the cerebellum and across the brain.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on known anatomical features.

claim: Reeler mice exhibited visible and severe gait ataxia when walking on the LocoMouse setup.
source: Reeler mice exhibited visible and severe gait ataxia when walking on the LocoMouse setup (Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments, supported by video evidence.

claim: Like pcd mice, reelers were smaller and walked more slowly than control littermates.
source: Like pcd mice (Machado et al., 2015), reelers were smaller and walked more slowly than control littermates (Materials and methods; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and comparison to prior work.

claim: The locomotor phenotypes of reeler and pcd mice were clearly distinguishable by eye, with reeler mice appearing much more severely ataxic than the mildly ataxic pcd mice.
source: However, the locomotor phenotypes of reeler and pcd mice were clearly distinguishable by eye, with reeler mice appearing much more severely ataxic than the mildly ataxic pcd mice (Video 1; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2019; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on visual observation supported by video and citations.

claim: The equations previously generated with mixed-effects linear models to predict stride parameters based on walking speed and body size were able to accurately predict the individual stride parameters of reeler mice.
source: First, the equations we previously generated with mixed-effects linear models (Machado et al., 2015) to predict stride parameters based on walking speed and body size were able to accurately predict the individual stride parameters (including stride length, cadence, stance duration) of reeler mice (Figure 1. E-G), as we had previously shown for pcd (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E-G and comparison to prior models.

claim: The continuous forward trajectories of reeler front paws were similar to those of size-matched controls, across walking speeds.
source: Moreover, the continuous forward trajectories of reeler front paws were similar to those of size-matched controls, across walking speeds (Figure 1H, top).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The forward trajectories of reeler hind paws exhibited lower forward velocities compared to size and speed-matched controls.
source: Notably, the forward trajectories of reeler hind paws exhibited lower forward velocities compared to size and speed-matched controls (Figure 1H, bottom), and they had accompanying increases in swing duration (from size-matched controls = 98.78 ± 6.48 ms to reeler = 114.72 ± 8.21 ms).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H and quantitative measurements.

claim: Reeler hind paws had accompanying increases in swing duration compared to size-matched controls (from 98.78 ± 6.48 ms to 114.72 ± 8.21 ms).
source: Notably, the forward trajectories of reeler hind paws exhibited lower forward velocities compared to size and speed-matched controls (Figure 1H, bottom), and they had accompanying increases in swing duration (from size-matched controls = 98.78 ± 6.48 ms to reeler = 114.72 ± 8.21 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: Comparison of 3D trajectories revealed clear differences between reeler and control mice in both the side-to-side and the vertical paw movements of both front and hind paws.
source: Comparison of 3D trajectories revealed clear differences between reeler and control mice in both the side-to-side and the vertical paw movements of both front and hind paws (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Reeler mice did not exhibit an increased width of base of support.
source: Finally, and perhaps surprisingly given their severe ataxia, reeler mice did not exhibit an increased width of base of support (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Both reeler and pcd exhibited altered 3D trajectories of all paws when compared to those of speed and size-matched controls.
source: Both reeler and pcd exhibited altered 3D trajectories of all paws when compared to those of speed and size-matched controls (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The off-axis (side-to-side and vertical) movements of all paws showed nearly identical alterations in reeler and pcd mutants.
source: In particular, the off-axis (side-to-side and vertical) movements of all paws showed nearly identical alterations in the two mutants (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: Forward hind paw trajectories were profoundly affected in reelers, while more subtle effects were seen on the forward movement of the front paws.
source: In addition, forward hind paw trajectories were profoundly affected in reelers, while more subtle effects were seen on the forward movement of the front paws (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Neither the front nor hind limb trajectories of pcd mice exhibited increased variability.
source: Despite their ataxia, neither the front nor hind limb trajectories of pcd mice exhibited increased variability (Figure 2H; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and prior publication.

claim: Paw movement was generally more variable in reeler, including the forward motion of the hind paws and the vertical movements of both front and hind paws.
source: Paw movement was generally more variable in reeler, including the forward motion of the hind paws (Figure 2H-bottom) and the vertical movements of both front and hind paws (Figure 2I-top and bottom).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Mice typically walk in a symmetrical trot pattern across a wide range of walking speeds.
source: Mice typically walk in a symmetrical trot pattern across a wide range of walking speeds (Figure 3A; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a known fact about mouse locomotion supported by data and citation.

claim: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination was markedly disrupted in reeler, due to specific and consistent changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs.
source: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination was markedly disrupted in reeler, due to specific and consistent changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The alterations in front-hind limb stance phasing in reelers were identical on average to those of pcd mice; in both mutants, hind paw touch downs were delayed relative to their diagonal partners.
source: Remarkably, the alterations in front-hind limb stance phasing in reelers were identical on average to those of pcd mice; in both mutants, hind paw touch downs were delayed relative to their diagonal partners (Figure 3B,C; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B,C and comparison to prior work.

claim: Relative left-right stance phasing of both the front and hind limbs was intact in both reelers and pcd.
source: In contrast, relative left-right stance phasing of both the front and hind limbs was intact in both reelers and pcd (Figure 3D; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and comparison to prior work.

claim: The front-hind limb phasing was more variable on average in reeler, but not pcd.
source: Consistent with the increased variability of hind limb movements, the front-hind limb phasing was more variable on average in reeler, but not pcd (size-matched controls = 0.25 ± 0.05%, pcd = 0.29 ± 0.09% F1,82 = 1.02, p=0.32, reeler = 0.48 ± 0.11% F1,82 = 5.79, **p=9.5×10−3), and left-right phasing was not more variable in either mutant (size-matched controls = 0.25 ± 0.06%, pcd = 0.19 ± 0.07% F1,54 = 0.23, p=0.63, reeler = 0.22 ± 0.07%, F1,74 = 0.11, p=0.75).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Left-right phasing was not more variable in either reeler or pcd mutant.
source: Consistent with the increased variability of hind limb movements, the front-hind limb phasing was more variable on average in reeler, but not pcd (size-matched controls = 0.25 ± 0.05%, pcd = 0.29 ± 0.09% F1,82 = 1.02, p=0.32, reeler = 0.48 ± 0.11% F1,82 = 5.79, **p=9.5×10−3), and left-right phasing was not more variable in either mutant (size-matched controls = 0.25 ± 0.06%, pcd = 0.19 ± 0.07% F1,54 = 0.23, p=0.63, reeler = 0.22 ± 0.07%, F1,74 = 0.11, p=0.75).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: At most natural walking speeds, wildtype mice typically have a single diagonal pair of paws on the ground at any given time.
source: At most natural walking speeds, wildtype mice typically have a single diagonal pair of paws on the ground at any given time (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a known fact about mouse locomotion supported by citation.

claim: Reeler mice exhibited an increase in 3-paw support patterns.
source: Reeler mice exhibited an increase in 3-paw support patterns (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Reeler mice spent more time in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support and 2-front paw supports.
source: They also spent more time in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support (Figure 3F) and 2-front paw supports (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Increased instability in support patterns is consistent with impaired interlimb coordination rather than a simple switch to a different gait pattern.
source: This increased instability was also observed in pcd (Machado et al., 2015) and is consistent with impaired interlimb coordination rather than a simple switch to a different gait pattern (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by data and citations.

claim: Reeler mice spent more time with both front paws on the ground than both controls and pcd.
source: In particular, reeler mice spent more time with both front paws on the ground than both controls and pcd, either as sole supports (Figure 3G), or as part of a 3 or four paw support configuration (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Reelers spent less time with both hind paws on the ground than pcd or control mice.
source: Interestingly, reelers also spent less time with both hind paws on the ground than pcd or control mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The ratio of front to hind paw double support was higher in reeler (0.43) than in pcd (0.14) and control mice (0.10).
source: The ratio of front to hind paw double support was higher in reeler (front/hind = 0.43) than in pcd (front/hind = 0.14) and control mice (front/hind = 0.10).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison derived from the data.

claim: Decreased hind paw double support in reeler is likely to be a consequence of the impaired hindlimb control.
source: This decreased hind paw double support is likely to be a consequence of the impaired hindlimb control described in Figure 1 and Figure 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in earlier figures.

claim: Like pcd, reeler mice exhibited large side-to-side oscillations of the tail and nose with respect to the stride cycle when compared to controls.
source: Like pcd (Machado et al., 2015), reeler mice exhibited large side-to-side oscillations of the tail and nose with respect to the stride cycle (Figure 4A–F, green) when compared to controls (black).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-F and comparison to prior work.

claim: In both reeler and pcd, both tail and nose movements became increasingly phase-lagged relative to the locomotor cycle at faster speeds.
source: Also like pcd, both tail (Figure 4A,C) and nose (Figure 4D,F) movements became increasingly phase-lagged relative to the locomotor cycle at faster speeds.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,C,D,F.

claim: The tail and nose movements of pcd mice could be successfully modelled as a passive consequence of hind limb movement.
source: We previously showed that the tail and nose movements of pcd mice could be successfully modelled as a passive consequence of hind limb movement (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: A model that converted hindlimb oscillation into nose and tail trajectories using solely the geometric relationships between body parts moving with fixed time delays accurately predicted the side-to-side tail and nose movements of pcd mice across walking speeds.
source: A model that converted hindlimb oscillation into nose and tail trajectories using solely the geometric relationships between body parts moving with fixed time delays accurately predicted the side-to-side tail and nose movements of pcd mice across walking speeds.
evidence: This refers to a model from prior work that successfully predicted pcd behavior.

claim: The specific phase relationships of both the tail and nose with respect to the locomotor cycle were dramatically different in reeler compared to pcd.
source: However, the specific phase relationships of both the tail and nose with respect to the locomotor cycle were dramatically different in reeler compared to pcd (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B,E.

claim: Aligning the reeler tail oscillations to the front limbs, rather than hind limbs, revealed that the phase relationship between the reeler tail and the front limbs was nearly identical to that of the pcd tail to the hind limbs.
source: To our surprise, simply aligning the reeler tail oscillations to the front limbs, rather than hind limbs (Figure 4C), immediately revealed that the phase relationship between the reeler tail and the front limbs was nearly identical to that of the pcd tail to the hind limbs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The tail movements of reeler mice have the same quantitative relationship to front limb movement that the pcd tail had to the hind limbs.
source: In other words, the tail movements of reeler mice have the same quantitative relationship to front limb movement that the pcd tail had to the hind limbs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Side-to-side nose movements in reeler were almost perfectly out of phase with the base of the tail.
source: Side-to-side nose movements in reeler were almost perfectly out of phase with the base of the tail (Figure 4F), suggesting that both the tail and nose movements of reeler mice oscillate along a single, straight body axis with each stride (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both the tail and nose movements of reeler mice oscillate along a single, straight body axis with each stride.
source: Side-to-side nose movements in reeler were almost perfectly out of phase with the base of the tail (Figure 4F), suggesting that both the tail and nose movements of reeler mice oscillate along a single, straight body axis with each stride (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phase relationship shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The shift of supports to front paws leads to the loss of a front-limb steering component in reeler.
source: One possible explanation for the differences in relative tail and nose phasing between pcd and reeler (Figure 4E) is that the shift of supports to front paws leads to the loss of a front-limb steering component in reeler (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Reelers, but not pcd, exhibited larger side-to-side movements of the body center while walking.
source: Consistent with this idea, reelers, but not pcd, exhibited larger side-to-side movements of the body center while walking (Figure 4H, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4H and Video 1.

claim: An analytical model that computed predicted lateral trajectories of the tail and nose directly from the forward-backward oscillations of the front limbs accurately reproduced the phases as well as the actual trajectories of the tail and nose of reeler mice, across a range of walking speeds.
source: The model output accurately reproduced the phases as well as the actual trajectories of the tail and nose of reeler mice, across a range of walking speeds (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the model predictions shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Hindlimb-driven models performed less well at predicting reeler tail and nose movements, even allowing for the possibility of substantially longer time delays.
source: Notably, hindlimb-driven models, although optimal for pcd (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I), performed less well at predicting reeler tail and nose movements, even allowing for the possibility of substantially longer time delays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This is supported by model comparisons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: A single body-axis model was not appropriate for the pcd data.
source: Similarly, unlike reeler, a single body-axis model was not appropriate for the pcd data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model fitting results.

claim: In reeler, like pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
source: Thus, in reeler, like pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: The altered phasing in the two mutants suggests that the shift in the support patterns towards the front paws in reeler causes the tail and body axis to oscillate as a passive consequence of the front, rather than hind limbs.
source: The altered phasing in the two mutants suggests that the shift in the support patterns towards the front paws in reeler (Figure 3, and presumably resulting from impaired hindlimb control shown in Figure 1) causes the tail and body axis to oscillate as a passive consequence of the front, rather than hind limbs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and modeling results.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis successfully captured meaningful differences in an abstract feature subspace to separate the three genotypes based on their locomotor phenotypes across walking speeds.
source: LDA successfully captured meaningful differences in an abstract feature subspace to separate the three genotypes based on their locomotor phenotypes across walking speeds (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the LDA results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Two distinct, orthogonal axes effectively separate controls from mutants (LD1), and the two mutants from each other (LD2).
source: Unexpectedly, this analysis revealed that two distinct, orthogonal axes effectively separate controls from mutants (LD1), and the two mutants from each other (LD2) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the LDA results shown in Figure 5.

claim: LD1, which separates controls from ataxic mutants, is highly influenced by variables representing 3D paw trajectories and interlimb and whole-body coordination.
source: Inspection of the contributions of each gait parameter to the two LDs reveals that LD1, which separates controls from ataxic mutants, is highly influenced by variables representing 3D paw trajectories and interlimb and whole-body coordination (Figure 5, x-axis bar graph).
evidence: This is supported by the contribution scores shown in Figure 5.

claim: The features contributing most strongly to LD2, which captured the differences in locomotor phenotype between the two mutants, included measurements of hindpaw movement, variability, and relative phase of tail/nose movements.
source: The features contributing most strongly to LD2, which captured the differences in locomotor phenotype between the two mutants, included measurements of hindpaw movement (and subsequent changes in support patterns), variability, and relative phase of tail/nose movements (Figure 5, y-axis bar graph).
evidence: This is supported by the contribution scores shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most variables relating to the averaged forward motion of individual limbs, which are largely spared in both mutants, do not strongly influence either LD.
source: Most variables relating to the averaged forward motion of individual limbs, which are largely spared in both mutants, do not strongly influence either LD.
evidence: This is an observation from the LDA contribution analysis.

claim: The LDA provides a quantitative summary that captures the essential elements of the similarities and differences in locomotor behavior across groups of mice.
source: The LDA provides a quantitative summary that captures the essential elements of the similarities and differences in locomotor behavior across groups of mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the utility of the LDA approach.

claim: A high-dimensional set of gait parameters contains a subspace of mixed features in which multiple neuropathologies are represented behaviorally.
source: In so doing, it shows that a high-dimensional set of gait parameters contains a subspace of mixed features in which multiple neuropathologies are represented behaviorally.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the LDA results.

claim: Multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination are shared, and possibly fundamental, features of locomotor ataxia.
source: The results, together with our previous description of the locomotor phenotype of pcd mice (Machado et al., 2015), reveal multijoint, interlimb, and whole-body coordination as shared, and possibly fundamental, features of locomotor ataxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results from this study and prior work.

claim: When assessing motor coordination deficits in mice there is often a tradeoff between specificity and interpretability.
source: When assessing motor coordination deficits in mice there is often a tradeoff between specificity and interpretability.
evidence: This is a general statement about methodological challenges in the field.

claim: Rotarod testing provides measurable and intuitive low dimensional outputs, but lacks specificity.
source: For example, approaches such as rotarod testing provide measurable and intuitive low dimensional outputs, but lack specificity.
evidence: This is a known limitation of rotarod testing.

claim: The CatWalk system can provide many detailed measurements of locomotor behavior, but their meaning is not always readily apparent.
source: Others, such as the CatWalk system (Gabriel et al., 2009) can provide many detailed measurements of locomotor behavior, but their meaning is not always readily apparent.
evidence: This is a critique of the CatWalk system supported by citation.

claim: LocoMouse provides both a comprehensive, quantitative description of locomotor behavior as well as a conceptual framework within which to interpret that high-dimensional data.
source: With LocoMouse we have tried to provide both a comprehensive, quantitative description of locomotor behavior as well as a conceptual framework within which to interpret that high-dimensional data.
evidence: This is a statement about the goals and capabilities of the LocoMouse system.

claim: The visible gait differences in reeler and pcd mutants appear to stem specifically from an increase in movement variability and additional hindlimb involvement in reelers.
source: Rather than simple differences in the level of severity in the same set of affected features, the visible gait differences in the two mutants (captured by the second linear discriminant) appear to stem specifically from an increase in movement variability and additional hindlimb involvement (Cendelin, 2014) in reelers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LDA and data analysis.

claim: Analysis of support patterns and nose and tail movements suggests that reelers, unlike controls and pcd, use their front paws as their main supports while walking.
source: As a likely consequence of those deficits, analysis of support patterns and nose and tail movements suggests that reelers, unlike controls and pcd, use their front paws as their main supports while walking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: The inability of reelers to walk in a straight line is likely because the front limbs are unable to provide both support and steering control to keep the body moving forward.
source: It could also explain the inability of reelers to walk in a straight line (Video 1, Figure 4H), likely because the front limbs are unable to provide both support and steering control to keep the body moving forward.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the observed behavior.

claim: In pcd, the main anatomical phenotype is cerebellar, with striking degeneration of Purkinje cells that effectively removes cerebellar cortical input to the cerebellar nuclei.
source: In pcd, the main anatomical phenotype is cerebellar, with striking degeneration of Purkinje cells that effectively removes cerebellar cortical input to the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is a known anatomical feature of pcd mice.

claim: Reeler mice exhibit aberrant cell localization throughout the brain, which could also contribute to their gait abnormalities.
source: In contrast, reeler mice exhibit aberrant cell localization throughout the brain (Terashima et al., 1983; Stanfield et al., 1979; Mikoshiba et al., 1980; Blatt and Eisenman, 1988; Kang et al., 2010), which could also contribute to their gait abnormalities.
evidence: This is a known anatomical feature of reeler mice supported by citations.

evidence: This is a known feature of reeler mice supported by citations.

claim: Locomotor differences between reeler and pcd mutants likely represent a combination of specific differences in circuitry within the cerebellum itself plus extracerebellar effects.
